research_question: What is moksha in Indian philosophical traditions? Examine its definitions, paths (margas), and liberation theories across major schools.

indic_traditions.scope: All Indian philosophical schools (Vedanta, Samkhya, Yoga, Buddhism, Jainism, Nyaya, Vaisheshika) on moksha - definitions, conditions, paths, and liberation theories
known_sources: Moksha in Buddhism — Four Noble Truths, Nirvana
Moksha in Nyaya — Liberation through valid knowledge
indic_traditions.special_instructions: IMPORTANT: Use SCRIPT TRIAD FORMAT for all citations: (1) Text Name, (2) Author/Compiler, (3) Verse/Section Number. Example: Bhagavad Gita 5.23-24 — Krishna (Moksha definition through yoga). Include original Sanskrit terms with transliteration.

western_philosophy.scope: Western philosophical concepts of liberation, freedom, and salvation that parallel or contrast with moksha
known_sources: Plato — Republic, Allegory of the Cave
Schopenhauer — Liberation through denial of will
western_philosophy.special_instructions: Focus on liberation/freedom concepts that parallel Indic ideas. Note where Western frameworks may fail to capture moksha nuance.

ancient_civilizations.scope: Ancient non-Indian civilization perspectives on liberation, afterlife, and transcendence
known_sources: Egyptian Book of the Dead — Afterlife journey
Greek mystery traditions — Eleusinian mysteries, Orphic liberation
Chinese Taoism — Wu wei, liberation from desire
Ancient Judaism — Olam Ha-Ba, world to come
ancient_civilizations.special_instructions: Identify structural parallels to moksha concepts while noting cultural specificity. Ancient Greco-Roman and Near Eastern focus.

contemporary_scholarship.scope: Modern academic scholarship on moksha, comparative philosophy, and interdisciplinary studies
known_sources: Princeton University Press — Hindu philosophy series
Oxford University Press — South Asian philosophy series
Julius Lipner — Hindus: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices
contemporary_scholarship.special_instructions: Focus on recent scholarship (post-2000) and interdisciplinary approaches. Include comparative religion, continental philosophy engagement, and cognitive science of religion perspectives.
